title: SPOF, failover, fault tolerance, reliability patterns
scopeHtml:
Scope: SPOFs, redundancy, failover and split brain, timeouts retries breakers, degradation, chaos.

Scope: SPOFs, redundancy, failover and split brain, timeouts retries breakers, degradation, chaos.

notes.title: Single points of failure
notes.html:
A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure stops the whole system. Find them by walking a request and asking at every box: "if this dies, what happens?"

Common hidden SPOFs: one load balancer, one database primary, one DNS provider, one config service, one cloud region, one certificate expiry date, one person who knows the deploy.

In the diagram, app servers are redundant, but the LB and database are each a single point. Fixes: LBs in pairs (active-passive with a floating IP or active-active behind DNS/anycast) and a database with a replica plus automated failover.

Worked example. App tier 3 instances (99.9% each, independent): 1 - 0.001^3 is effectively 100%. One DB at 99.95%. System is limited by the DB: 99.95%, about 4.4 hours of downtime a year. Adding a standby with automatic failover (30 s) shifts the limit to failover time and bugs.

Industry examples. The 2021 Facebook outage: DNS and BGP configuration became a SPOF, locking engineers out of internal tools too. Many AWS us-east-1 incidents hit teams that were in one region only.

Everyday analogy. A bridge that is the only road to town.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing two app servers and calling it "highly available" while one DB remains.
  • Forgetting control-plane SPOFs: auth service, config, service discovery, CI/CD.

notes.title: Redundancy models: active-passive and active-active
notes.html:
Redundancy means spare capacity in a different failure domain. Two models.

  • Active-passive (hot or warm standby): one serves, one waits. Simple; failover takes seconds to minutes; standby capacity is idle (cost). Used for primary databases.
  • Active-active: all serve traffic. Better utilisation and instant loss tolerance; needs data conflict handling and N+1 capacity planning.
  • Cold standby: restore from backup; hours of recovery; cheap.

Decision gravity. Active-passive is simple and mostly reversible. Active-active for stateful data (multi-writer) is a one-way door: you must design conflict resolution (last write wins, CRDTs, partition ownership) up front.

Capacity rule N+1 / N+2. If 3 nodes carry the load at 60% each, losing 1 puts survivors at 90%, so plan N+1 beyond peak, or accept degraded mode.

Worked example. 3 AZs, each holding 33% of traffic at 50% CPU. Losing one AZ shifts the load to 2 AZs at 75% CPU. Fine. With 2 AZs at 70% CPU, losing one means 140%: outage. Rule: with k zones, keep each zone below (k-1)/k of capacity.

Industry examples. Postgres streaming replication with Patroni/pg_auto_failover is active-passive; Cassandra and DynamoDB are active-active across nodes. Route 53 health-checked DNS and anycast (Cloudflare) provide LB redundancy.

Everyday analogy. A spare tyre (active-passive) versus a car with four drivers all driving shifts (active-active).

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting N+1 capacity: redundancy without headroom still fails.
  • Redundant components in the same rack or AZ sharing power.

notes.title: Failover: detection, election, switch
notes.html:
Failover is moving work from a failed node to a healthy one. Three steps: detect, decide, switch.

  1. Detect: heartbeats (for example every 1 s, declare dead after 3 misses), health checks, or lease expiry.
  2. Decide: who becomes primary? Use a consensus system (etcd, ZooKeeper, Raft) so there is exactly one leader.
  3. Switch: move the virtual IP, update DNS or service discovery, promote the replica, reconnect clients.

Split brain is the danger: a network partition makes both nodes think they are primary, and both accept writes, diverging data. Defences: quorum (majority) voting, fencing (STONITH, lease tokens, epoch numbers so the old primary's writes are rejected), and requiring an odd number of voters (3 or 5).

RTO and RPO: RTO = how long you can be down; RPO = how much data you can lose. Async replication gives low latency but RPO > 0 (acknowledged writes lost on failover). Sync replication gives RPO = 0 but higher write latency and lower availability if the replica is down.

Worked example. Postgres with Patroni: heartbeat to etcd every 10 s with ttl 30 s; failover about 30 to 45 s; async replica lag 100 ms means up to 100 ms of writes may be lost (RPO). Sync mode (synchronous_commit = on with a sync standby) raises commit latency from 1 ms to about 3 ms in the same AZ but RPO = 0.

Industry examples. GitHub's 2018 outage: a 43-second network partition caused cross-region MySQL failover with replication gaps; restoring consistency took about a day. Lesson: failover itself is risky, and automatic failover can create data divergence.

Everyday analogy. A relay baton: the runner must hand it off cleanly; two runners holding it is chaos.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring split brain.
  • Claiming zero downtime and zero data loss at the same time with async replication.
  • Not testing failover; untested failover usually fails.

notes.title: Reliability patterns: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers
notes.html:
Calls to other services will fail or hang. These patterns stop one slow dependency from killing everyone.

  • Timeouts: always set one, shorter than the caller's own budget (for example client 2 s, service-to-service 500 ms, DB 200 ms). No timeout means threads pile up forever.
  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter: wait 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms plus random jitter; cap attempts (2 or 3) and only retry idempotent operations.
  • Circuit breaker: after N failures in a window (for example 50% of 20 calls), open the circuit and fail fast for 30 s, then half-open to test.
  • Bulkhead: separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency so one cannot drain all.
  • Rate limiting and load shedding: reject early when overloaded to keep latency for the rest.
  • Idempotency keys: make retries safe.
// Resilience4j style (illustrative values; confirm API in docs)
CircuitBreakerConfig cfg = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .failureRateThreshold(50)
    .slidingWindowSize(20)
    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .build();

Retry storm math. 3 layers each retrying 3 times means 3^3 = 27 requests for one user action at the bottom. Retry at only one layer, or use retry budgets (retries <= 10% of requests).

Worked example. Service A calls B with 3 retries and no jitter. B slows; all A instances retry in lockstep every 100 ms. B load triples and never recovers. Fix: jitter, 2 attempts, circuit breaker, retry budget.

Industry examples. Netflix Hystrix (now maintenance mode) popularised breakers; Resilience4j, Envoy, Istio and AWS SDKs implement them. Google SRE book chapter on cascading failures covers retry budgets.

Decision gravity. These are configuration choices, easily reversible, but a wrong default (infinite timeout, unlimited retries) is a common root cause.

Everyday analogy. A fuse box: trip a breaker to protect the house rather than burn down.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying non-idempotent calls (double charge).
  • Retries at every layer.
  • No jitter, so clients synchronise.

notes.title: Graceful degradation and fault tolerance
notes.html:
Fault tolerance means the system keeps working (maybe worse) despite component failures. Graceful degradation means giving a reduced but useful service instead of a total failure.

Examples:

  • Recommendations service down: show popular items from a static list.
  • Search down: show cached results or browse mode.
  • Payment provider slow: queue the order and confirm later.
  • Reads from stale cache when DB is unreachable (serve with a "stale" flag).

Design tools: feature flags and kill switches, fallbacks, default values, queue-based decoupling, static fallback pages on a CDN, read-only mode.

Worked example. Product page calls 6 services. Only price and inventory are critical; reviews, recommendations, ads are optional with 100 ms budget and fallback. Page availability becomes that of 2 services, not 6: from 0.999^6 = 99.4% to 0.999^2 = 99.8%.

Industry examples. Netflix falls back to non-personalised rows when recommendations fail. Twitter's "fail whale" era led to heavy investment in degradation. Amazon retail uses static fallbacks and feature isolation.

Decision gravity. Marking a dependency "optional" is a product decision; mistakes are visible to users but reversible.

Everyday analogy. A shop whose card machine is down still takes cash.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating every dependency as critical.
  • Returning errors where a stale or default value would do.

notes.title: Health checks, redundancy across failure domains and chaos testing
notes.html:
Know the failure domains: process, host, rack, AZ, region, provider. Spread replicas across them, then verify by killing things.

  • Liveness vs readiness checks: liveness = process alive (restart if not); readiness = ready for traffic (warm cache, DB connected). Kubernetes probes: avoid liveness checks that depend on downstream services, or one dependency outage restarts every pod.
  • Deep vs shallow health checks: deep checks (touch the DB) detect more but can cause cascading removal from the LB when the DB hiccups.
  • Chaos engineering: kill instances, inject latency, drain an AZ in production-like environments (Chaos Monkey, Gremlin, AWS FIS).
  • Backups and restore drills: a backup you never restored is a hope.
# Kubernetes probes (illustrative values)
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2

Worked example. Liveness probe checks the DB. DB blips for 40 s; all pods fail liveness and restart together; cold caches then hammer the recovering DB. Fix: liveness checks only the process itself; readiness controls traffic.

Industry examples. Netflix Simian Army, Google DiRT (disaster recovery testing) exercises, AWS game days.

Everyday analogy. Fire drills: you find the blocked exit before the fire.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the same endpoint for liveness and readiness.
  • Never practising restore or failover.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Find SPOFs by asking "if this dies?" at every box, including LB, DB, DNS, region and control plane.
  • Redundancy: active-passive (simple) vs active-active (needs conflict handling); keep N+1 capacity.
  • Failover = detect, elect, switch; guard against split brain with quorum and fencing; state RTO/RPO.
  • Use timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, idempotency, load shedding.
  • Degrade gracefully; mark optional dependencies optional.
  • Spread across failure domains, separate liveness from readiness, and test with chaos and restore drills.

questions.promptHtml: What is a single point of failure and how do you find them in a design?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every HA design review starts here; candidates who only duplicate app servers miss the real ones.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A SPOF is any component whose failure takes the whole system down. I find them by walking a request path and asking at every box "if this dies, what happens?" The usual suspects are the load balancer, the database primary, DNS, a config or auth service, a single region, an expiring certificate, and even a single person who knows how to deploy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client -> LB -> App x3 -> DB primary
              (redundant)   (SPOF)

Three app instances at 99.9% give about 100% for that tier, but one DB at 99.95% caps the system at 99.95%, about 4.4 h/year. Fixes: LB pairs (floating IP, or anycast/DNS), DB replica with automated failover, then ask the same question of the failover mechanism itself. Control-plane SPOFs matter: auth, service discovery, CI/CD, secrets. The 2021 Facebook outage showed DNS/BGP configuration becoming a SPOF that also locked engineers out of internal tools.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Two app servers and "highly available" with one database.
  • Forgetting control-plane and human SPOFs.
  • Redundant components that share a rack, power or AZ.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a replica enough to remove the DB SPOF? -> Only with detection, election and switch automated and tested.
  2. Is a cloud region a SPOF? -> Yes, for tier-1 services that must survive region loss.
  3. Can a certificate be a SPOF? -> Yes: expiry takes everything down at once; monitor and automate renewal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: duplicate servers. Senior: walks the whole path including control plane, humans and shared fate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Outages from expired certificates and single DNS providers are common and boring.

questions.promptHtml: Compare active-passive and active-active redundancy. When would you pick each, and what is the N+1 rule?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests trade-off thinking and whether you account for capacity, not just copies.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Active-passive: one node serves, a standby waits; simple, failover takes seconds to minutes, standby is idle cost. It fits primary databases. Active-active: all nodes serve; better utilisation and near-instant loss tolerance, but stateful data needs conflict handling. N+1 means I provision enough that after losing one node the survivors still carry peak load.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Active-passive hot/warm: seconds to minutes; cold: restore from backup, hours.
  • Active-active for stateless tiers is easy; for multi-writer state it is a one-way door: pick a conflict strategy (last write wins, CRDTs, partition ownership) up front.
  • Capacity: 3 nodes at 60% each, lose one, survivors at 90%. 2 zones at 70% each, lose one: 140%, an outage. With k zones keep each below (k-1)/k of capacity. Examples: Postgres with Patroni is active-passive; Cassandra and DynamoDB are active-active across nodes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Redundancy with no spare capacity.
  • Same rack or AZ for "redundant" nodes.
  • Calling multi-region active-active "free".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is multi-writer a one-way door? -> Data model and conflict semantics get baked into the application.
  2. Cost of active-passive? -> Idle standby capacity (can serve reads if designed so).
  3. When is cold standby fine? -> Non-critical systems where hours of recovery is acceptable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definitions. Senior: capacity math and the data-conflict gravity.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "We have two nodes" outages where one node could not carry the load.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through a database failover end to end. What is split brain and how is it prevented? How do RTO and RPO fit in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Failover is where HA designs actually break; data divergence is the worst failure mode.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Three steps: detect (heartbeats, health checks, lease expiry), decide (consensus such as etcd or Raft picks exactly one leader), switch (promote the replica, move the VIP or DNS, reconnect clients). Split brain is two nodes both believing they are primary and accepting writes. I prevent it with quorum, odd voter counts, and fencing so the old primary cannot write. RTO is how long I can be down; RPO is how much data I can lose: async replication gives RPO greater than zero, sync gives zero at a latency and availability cost.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Primary fails -> missed heartbeats -> quorum elects new leader
              -> fence old primary (STONITH, lease, epoch token)
              -> promote replica -> repoint clients

Patroni example: ttl 30 s, heartbeat every 10 s, failover about 30 to 45 s; async lag of 100 ms means up to 100 ms of acknowledged writes may be lost. Synchronous commit with a sync standby gives RPO 0 and raises commit latency, for example from about 1 ms to 3 ms in-AZ (illustrative). GitHub's 2018 incident: a 43 second partition triggered failover with a replication gap, and reconciliation took about a day.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Patroni-style settings (illustrative, verify names for your version)
ttl: 30
loop_wait: 10
retry_timeout: 10
synchronous_mode: false

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring split brain.
  • Promising zero downtime and zero data loss with async replication.
  • Never testing failover.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why odd voter counts? -> A majority always exists in one side of a partition.
  2. What is fencing? -> Making the old primary unable to write: kill power, revoke a lease, reject old epoch tokens at storage.
  3. Is faster detection always better? -> No; aggressive timeouts cause false failovers on a GC pause or network blip.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "promote the replica". Senior: quorum, fencing, RTO/RPO with numbers and the false-positive trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Automatic failover that created two writable primaries and a day of data reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: Design review for a new B2B API. The proposal: 3 app pods across 3 AZs behind a cloud load balancer; one Postgres instance with nightly backups; Redis single node for sessions; auth through a company SSO service reached on every request; secrets fetched at startup from a single vault; DNS at one provider; TLS certificate renewed manually each year; deployments by a script run from one engineer's laptop. Target 99.95%.
questions.promptHtml: List the SPOFs, rank them, and say what you would change first.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a replica for the database" and stop.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is RPO and RTO? Is session loss acceptable? Can auth tokens be validated locally (JWT) or must each call hit SSO? Is the vault needed after startup?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; prioritise.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked by blast radius times likelihood: (1) Postgres single instance: hard data and downtime, restore from nightly backup means hours and up to 24 h of data loss. (2) Sync call to SSO on every request: inherits its availability, in series. (3) Redis single node: sessions lost on failure (users logged out). (4) Manual certificate: a calendar-driven total outage. (5) DNS single provider. (6) Vault at startup: only matters if pods restart during an outage. (7) Laptop deploy: human SPOF.
  4. How I'd verify: Walk the request path with the team, and a "kill each box" tabletop; compute availability: DB 99.95% x SSO 99.9% x Redis 99.9% is about 99.75% before anything else.
  5. Root cause: Redundancy exists only in the stateless tier.
  6. Fix: DB with replica and automated failover (RPO/RTO stated, PITR backups); validate JWTs locally with cached keys and a short fallback; Redis replica or managed multi-AZ; automated cert renewal with expiry alert; second DNS provider if the SLO needs it; CI/CD pipeline deploys.
  7. Prevention: SPOF checklist in design template; game days.
  8. Trade-offs: Each fix costs money and complexity; I would do DB, auth path and certs first, and defer second DNS until the SLO demands it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is the cloud LB a SPOF? -> Managed LBs are multi-AZ; its SLA is a series term.
  • Single region? -> Acceptable at 99.95%; revisit at four nines.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-built cluster went down for hours when a manually renewed certificate expired on a holiday.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes only the DB.
  • Hire: finds auth, cert and Redis too.
  • Strong hire: ranks, computes series availability and sequences the work.

questions.contextHtml:
Code review of a payment client:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Response charge(Order o) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        try {
            return http.post("/charge", o);   // no timeout set
        } catch (Exception e) {
            Thread.sleep(100);                // fixed delay
        }
    }
    throw new PaymentFailed();
}
fun charge(o: Order): Response {
    repeat(5) {
        try { return http.post("/charge", o) }   // no timeout set
        catch (e: Exception) { Thread.sleep(100) }
    }
    throw PaymentFailed()
}

The service sits in a call chain: gateway (3 retries) -> orders (this code) -> payments provider.
questions.promptHtml: List every problem and the corrected design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use exponential backoff" and nothing else.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the charge endpoint idempotent? What is the caller's deadline? Which exceptions are retryable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; block the merge.
  3. Problems, ranked: (a) No timeout: a hung call blocks a thread indefinitely. (b) Retries a non-idempotent charge: a timeout after the provider charged leads to a double charge. (c) Fixed 100 ms delay, no jitter: clients retry in lockstep. (d) Retries on every Exception, including 4xx such as card declined. (e) 5 attempts here times 3 at the gateway = 15 calls per user action (multiplication across layers). (f) No circuit breaker or budget.
  4. How I'd verify: Fault injection: slow the provider to 10 s and count calls and threads.
  5. Root cause: Reliability code written as a loop, not a policy.
  6. Fix: Timeout shorter than the caller's budget (for example 800 ms with a 2 s client deadline), an idempotency key per order so retries are safe, 2 attempts at most with exponential backoff plus jitter, retry only on timeouts and 5xx, circuit breaker, and retry at one layer (or a 10% retry budget).
  7. Prevention: Shared client library with safe defaults; lint for missing timeouts.
  8. Trade-offs: Fewer retries means more visible failures but protects the provider and avoids storms; I would not retry blindly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Provider has no idempotency support? -> Query by order id before retrying or do not retry; make the outcome reconcilable.
  • Breaker opens during a provider blip? -> Fail fast with a queued retry later.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A missing idempotency key turned a 30 s provider slowdown into several hundred double charges.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: backoff only.
  • Hire: timeout, idempotency, jitter, retry limit.
  • Strong hire: spots multiplication across layers and proposes a budget.

questions.contextHtml:
Kubernetes deployment of 40 pods. The liveness probe calls /healthz, which runs SELECT 1 against Postgres (periodSeconds 10, failureThreshold 3). The DB had a 40 second failover. Events:

10:14:05 db primary unreachable
10:14:35 40/40 pods: Liveness probe failed -> Killing container
10:14:50 40 pods restarting; 0 ready endpoints; 503 from ingress
10:15:10 db new primary ready (35 s)
10:15:20 pods up, cache cold, DB CPU 100%, connection errors
10:19:40 recovery
questions.promptHtml: Why did a 40 s DB blip become a 5 minute outage and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the probe timeout."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are liveness and readiness the same endpoint? Do pods hold local warm caches? Is the DB failover time expected?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause kubelet restarts by patching the probe or scaling slowly; keep traffic gated by readiness.
  3. Hypotheses: (a) liveness depends on a downstream (confirmed by timing); (b) restart storm plus cold caches overloading the DB; (c) red herring: DB failover 35 s was within design.
  4. How I'd verify: kubectl describe pod events, probe config, timing of kills vs DB state.
  5. Root cause: A shared dependency in the liveness check restarts the whole fleet at once; recovery then hits a cold cache and DB.
  6. Fix: Liveness checks only the process (event loop responsive); readiness checks dependencies and removes a pod from traffic without killing it; add a startup probe; stagger and rate-limit cache refill; connection retry with jitter.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test: inject DB downtime in staging and assert no restarts.
  8. Trade-offs: Deep readiness checks can eject every pod at once too, so serve degraded or stale content rather than 503 where possible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Process deadlocks but port open? -> Liveness should exercise an internal heartbeat, not just the TCP port.
  • Should readiness fail when the DB is down? -> Only if the pod cannot serve anything useful; otherwise degrade.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dependency-aware liveness probe turned each downstream blip into a full restart and a self-inflicted thundering herd.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes timeouts.
  • Hire: separates liveness from readiness.
  • Strong hire: addresses cold-cache stampede and the deep-check trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: Explain timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers and bulkheads. How do they work together and how do they go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are the standard defences against cascading failure, and misconfigured defaults are a leading root cause.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A timeout bounds how long I wait, shorter than my caller's own budget. A retry with exponential backoff and jitter handles transient failures, limited to 2 or 3 attempts and only for idempotent calls. A circuit breaker opens after a failure rate threshold and fails fast so a sick dependency can recover. A bulkhead gives each dependency its own pool so one cannot drain everything. Wrongly combined, retries multiply: 3 layers of 3 retries is 27 calls for one user action.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Breaker: Closed -> (failure rate > 50% of 20 calls) -> Open (fail fast 30 s)
         -> Half-open (probe) -> Closed
Budgets: client 2 s > service call 500 ms > DB 200 ms
Backoff: 100, 200, 400 ms + random jitter

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
// Resilience4j style (illustrative, confirm API in the docs)
CircuitBreakerConfig cfg = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .failureRateThreshold(50)
    .slidingWindowSize(20)
    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .build();
// Resilience4j style (illustrative, confirm API in the docs)
val cfg = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .failureRateThreshold(50f)
    .slidingWindowSize(20)
    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .build()

Retry budgets (retries at most about 10% of requests) keep a struggling dependency from being buried. Idempotency keys make retries safe. Load shedding rejects early to protect latency for accepted requests.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No timeout (threads pile up).
  • Retries at every layer, no jitter, so clients synchronise.
  • Retrying non-idempotent operations.
  • Breaker with no fallback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why jitter? -> Without it all clients retry at the same instant and recreate the spike.
  2. Breaker vs bulkhead? -> Breaker stops calls to a failing dependency; bulkhead limits the resources it can consume.
  3. Where should retries live? -> One layer, usually closest to the failure, with a budget.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists patterns. Senior: gives the budget ordering, the 27x multiplication and the idempotency requirement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Retry storms and infinite timeouts are among the most common outage root causes.

questions.contextHtml: A product page calls six services: price, inventory, reviews, recommendations, ads, personalisation. Each is 99.9% available. Today any failure returns a 500 for the page. Page latency budget is 400 ms. Product owner says all six are "important".
questions.promptHtml: How do you design the page for failure and what is the availability gain?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds retries on all six calls.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the user buy without reviews or ads? What does a stale price cost? What is acceptable for an empty slot?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make non-critical calls non-blocking with short timeouts.
  3. Hypotheses: Treating all six as critical multiplies availability: 0.999^6 = 99.4%.
  4. How I'd verify: Fault-inject each dependency and confirm the page still renders.
  5. Reasoning: Only price and inventory are required, so the page is 0.999^2 = 99.8%.
  6. Fix: Optional sections with 100 ms budgets and fallbacks: popular items for recommendations, cached reviews, empty ad slot, default personalisation; a feature flag per section; cached last-known price only if the business accepts staleness and flags it.
  7. Prevention: Dependency criticality table reviewed with product; chaos tests of optional services.
  8. Trade-offs: Degraded pages can hide a broken dependency, so monitor fallback rate as its own SLI. I would not serve a stale price at checkout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Inventory is down? -> Allow browsing, block or warn on purchase, or accept backorder if the business agrees.
  • Fallback rate is 30% for hours? -> Alert; degradation must not become the silent norm.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Marking reviews optional took the page from three nines to nearly four with no new infrastructure.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries.
  • Hire: critical vs optional with fallbacks.
  • Strong hire: computes the gain, monitors fallback rate, keeps price integrity.

questions.contextHtml:
Inventory service: normal 3,000 req/s, capacity 5,000 req/s. At 11:02 a slow query pushed p50 to 900 ms for 30 seconds, then the query was fixed. Metrics:

11:02 inventory req/s 3000, errors 2% timeouts (client timeout 1 s)
11:03 inventory req/s 11800, errors 61%
11:06 inventory req/s 12100, errors 64%     (root cause fixed at 11:03)
clients: 3 attempts, 100 ms fixed backoff, no breaker, on 3 layers (app, gateway, mesh)

The query fix is deployed and healthy but the service does not recover.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it stay down after the trigger is gone and how do you recover and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale it up", or restarts it repeatedly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where are the retries (which layers)? Is traffic from real users or amplified? Can we shed load at the gateway?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut the incoming load: rate-limit or return 503 at the edge, disable retries via config, then let traffic ramp.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) retry amplification: layers retrying 3x each (up to 27x); (b) lockstep retries from fixed backoff; (c) the original slow query (ruled out, fixed at 11:03); (d) red herring: DB.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare request rate with unique client calls; check the retry count header or mesh stats.
  5. Root cause: A metastable failure: the system is overloaded because of retries, and retries persist while it is overloaded. 3,000 x about 4 = 12,000 req/s against 5,000 capacity.
  6. Fix: Short term: shed at the edge, temporarily disable retries, scale only after load is cut, then ramp slowly. Long term: single-layer retries, exponential backoff with jitter, retry budget of 10%, circuit breakers, server-side load shedding and queue limits, deadline propagation.
  7. Prevention: Load test with a slow-dependency injection; alert on request amplification (outgoing/incoming ratio).
  8. Trade-offs: Shedding drops good requests to save the system; I would not just add servers, because retry volume scales with capacity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mobile apps retry forever? -> Exponential backoff in the client, server Retry-After, and a kill switch.
  • Why did scaling not help? -> Demand was manufactured by the retries and grows as latency rises.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 30 second blip became a 40 minute outage until the edge was throttled to a fraction of normal traffic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales or restarts.
  • Hire: identifies retry amplification and sheds load.
  • Strong hire: names metastable failure, budgets, deadlines, amplification metric.

questions.contextHtml:
MySQL pair with async replication across two zones and automatic failover by an orchestrator that uses a simple 5 second ping from one monitor host. At 09:40 a 45 second network blip isolates the monitor from the primary, though the primary remains reachable by the app servers in its own zone.

09:40:05 monitor: primary unreachable x5 -> promoting replica (lag 1.8 s)
09:40:11 replica promoted, VIP moved
09:40:12 old primary still accepting writes from zone-A apps (did not receive demote)
09:40:50 network healed: two writable primaries, about 2.1k divergent writes on each
09:55    both frozen; support receives duplicate-order tickets
questions.promptHtml: What failed in the design and how do you recover and prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use synchronous replication" only, or "restart the old primary".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which writes diverged? Are keys auto-increment (collisions)? Is there a binlog position on both? How are clients routed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make exactly one node writable (fence the other, read-only), stop writers, snapshot both before touching anything.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) detector is a single vantage point and a partition looks like a death; (b) no fencing of the old primary; (c) no quorum; (d) red herring: replica lag of 1.8 s only explains lost writes, not the divergence.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare binlog positions and GTIDs; run a row-level diff on key tables since 09:40:05.
  5. Root cause: Failure detection without quorum or fencing allowed two primaries.
  6. Fix: Reconcile: choose the survivor (usually the promoted one), replay or manually merge unique writes from the other, regenerate or remap colliding ids, customer-facing reconciliation for orders. Long term: consensus-based leader election with 3 or 5 voters across failure domains (Patroni with etcd, Orchestrator with Raft, or managed HA), fencing via lease/epoch token or STONITH, semi-sync replication to bound loss, and a longer detection threshold to avoid false failovers.
  7. Prevention: Failover drills including partition cases; alert on two nodes reporting writable.
  8. Trade-offs: Semi-sync adds commit latency and can stall writes when the replica is down; I would not claim zero loss and zero downtime together.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not fail over faster? -> Faster detection increases false positives on blips; GitHub's 2018 incident shows failover itself can hurt.
  • Can the app help? -> Writes carry a fencing token or term number that storage rejects when stale.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A brief partition produced two primaries and a day of reconciliation; afterwards the team insisted on quorum-based election and fencing before any auto-failover.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts nodes.
  • Hire: fences, picks one primary, reconciles.
  • Strong hire: quorum, fencing token, semi-sync trade-off, drills.

questions.contextHtml: A booking service has Postgres primary in region A with an async replica in region B (active-passive, RTO 15 min, RPO about 5 s). Leadership wants "multi-region active-active" so that a region loss is invisible, within two quarters. 40% of traffic is in region B's geography. Data: user profiles (rarely edited), bookings with inventory counts that must not oversell, an audit log.
questions.promptHtml: How do you approach the migration and what do you say about "active-active"?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a multi-master database and flip the switch."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the business need: lower latency in B, survive region loss, or both? Can inventory be partitioned by hotel/city? What overselling tolerance exists? RPO/RTO targets?
  2. Immediate mitigation: First tighten the current model: automated failover, tested runbook, bring RTO from 15 to maybe 2 to 5 minutes.
  3. Hypotheses (options): (a) improved active-passive; (b) active-active for stateless tiers, read replicas locally, writes to home region; (c) partition ownership: each booking entity has a home region, so writes are single-writer per entity; (d) true multi-writer with conflict resolution (CRDTs, last-write-wins).
  4. How I'd verify: Classify each dataset by conflict risk: profiles tolerate LWW; the audit log is append-only and mergeable; inventory counts do not tolerate concurrent writers without coordination.
  5. Root cause of the difficulty: Multi-writer stateful data forces conflict semantics into the data model: a one-way door.
  6. Plan: Phase 1: active-active app tier, region-local reads, global traffic routing, keep one write region with automated failover. Phase 2: partition by home region for bookings (entity-level ownership), with a documented failover of ownership. Phase 3: only use LWW or CRDT for data where merges are safe. Dual-run and shadow traffic before cutover; reversible step by step.
  7. Prevention: Region-evacuation game days; conflict metrics.
  8. Trade-offs: True active-active cost and complexity may be worth it only if the business pays for four-plus nines. I would not promise it for inventory with LWW.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cross-region sync replication? -> RPO 0 but write latency includes the inter-region RTT (tens of ms; verify) and availability falls if the link does.
  • Two users book the last room in two regions? -> Needs a single owner for that inventory, or a reservation protocol; otherwise accept oversell with compensation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team moved a counter to LWW multi-master and lost increments silently for weeks before partitioned ownership replaced it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips to multi-master.
  • Hire: classifies data and proposes phases.
  • Strong hire: questions the requirement, improves RTO first, partitions ownership.

questions.contextHtml:
A drill, finally scheduled after a near miss: restore last night's production Postgres backup (1.8 TB) into staging. Findings:

00:00 start restore from nightly snapshot
00:20 restore finished: error "WAL segment 000000010000004A000000F3 missing"
02:40 second attempt from previous snapshot: ok, but 6 h 10 min total
backups bucket: same account and region as production; delete role shared with the app deploy role
alerts: backup job "success" alerts only on exit code; no restore ever tested

Stated RTO is 1 hour, RPO 5 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: What does this tell you and what do you do about it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fix the missing WAL file and move on."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why was the WAL missing (archiving gap, retention)? How is RTO defined, including detection and decision time? Who can delete backups?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take a verified fresh base backup now and check WAL archiving continuity.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) WAL archiving failed silently; (b) backup verification absent; (c) restore speed lower than the RTO by 6x; (d) red herring: the snapshot size alone.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_verifybackup, archive continuity check, time each restore phase, check IAM for who can delete.
  5. Root cause: The backup was trusted without ever restoring it; a backup you never restored is a hope.
  6. Fix: Automated daily restore test with integrity check and a success alert only on a verified restore; monitor WAL archive lag; copy backups to a second account and region with immutability (object lock); separate delete permissions; speed work: PITR with a warm replica or snapshots, parallel restore; renegotiate RTO honestly or invest (a replica with failover gives minutes, a restore never will).
  7. Prevention: Quarterly game days (restore, AZ drain, failover) with outcomes tracked as action items.
  8. Trade-offs: Verified restores cost compute and engineer time; the cost of finding out during a real incident is far larger. I would not report RTO 1 hour while measuring 6 hours.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ransomware deletes backups with the app role? -> Immutable, cross-account copies with separate credentials.
  • Chaos in production? -> Start in staging, then small blast radius in prod with abort conditions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company discovered during a real outage that its backups had been empty for months; restore drills would have taken an afternoon.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes the single error.
  • Hire: automates restore verification and measures real RTO.
  • Strong hire: adds immutability, separation of duties, honest RTO and drill cadence.
